Exact Balto-Slavic numeral and year phrase, but ordinary calendrical counting. Different narrative and solar contexts give no distinctive inherited poetic formula.
Russian negative enumeration of father, mother and kin is not Latvian maternal relatives becoming strangers; the cognates have different syntactic relations.
The Russian hoofprint encountered on the road is not the Vedic goat ritual or frog simile; the apparent second cognate is an unrelated use of falling, not a preserved pair.
Russian darkness and cognate repetition have no counterpart in Latin fearing and a new husband; no shared syntax.
Russian ribs beaten by an enemy and a Norse weapon flying between ribs share an anatomical term but no cognate verb or distinctive phrase.
Russian appeal to a dead mother to rise and wake differs from Bhima refusing to wake sleeping mother and brothers. Sleep-root correspondence alone is insufficient.
Ordinary dwelling vocabulary; Russian житьё-бытьё and Latin fit ... uiuimus do not share a syntactic figure, and the contexts differ.

near_miss.why_not: Search for Latin fumus + uoluo returned the Lucretius locus. Russian smoke is generally subject of an intransitive verb, while Latin fumum is object of uoluit. The natural movement of smoke and modern gunfire contexts do not establish inherited wording.

Cognate star and sky words are genuine, but locative star-in-sky and ablative falling-from-sky differ. Russian negative parallelism represents news or another event; Latvian has a star falling into the sea. Corpus testing does not isolate a distinctive shared figure beyond the familiar meteor image.

Exact cognate colour plus anatomical term with neck-to-mane specialization. Corpus search also finds Sanskrit black-necked horses (MBh 7.22.s42), but variable species and naturally black neck hair make independent formation easy. Russian collapsing onto the mane is not shared by Sanskrit gift, chariot-team or omen descriptions; insufficient evidence for inherited poetic wording.

Mead and guest roots occur in a congruent hospitality scene, but Russian guest is embedded in a derived verb; Norse gives mead to guests. Ordinary hospitality language and late transmission do not discriminate inheritance from independent wording.

Cognate honey and sweetness roots, but Latvian nominal sweetness-of-honey contrasts bitter hops in marriage, whereas Russian sweet mead is a literal drink epithet. Sanskrit search supports the general honey/sweet association, not a distinctive shared construction; sweetness is intrinsic to honey.

near_miss.lead: Tongue and teeth as a barrier to speech
near_miss.why_not: Russian injunction to keep silent and Vedic protection against destructive jaws/tongue use cognate body parts in different figures. Homeric fence-of-teeth is semantically closer, but its teeth word is not cognate with Russian зуб and tongue is replaced by utterance; no defensible inherited cognate pair.
Ordinary kin enumeration in a soldier exhortation versus a Christian threat involving parents and fosterers. No shared ordering or distinctive syntactic figure.
Avestan gaēϑā refers to living possessions/livestock taken by thief or wolf, not a living wolf. Another Serbian Vuk is a personal name; mapping overlap is not a collocation.

Serbian courtyard and Avestan duuarata are not demonstrated here as a shared noun phrase; Avestan passage is an apotropaic sequence. The automatic dvarə/dvarəm lemma on duuarata needs checking before any etymological comparison; not treated as secure.
Norse hringi and lyngva occur in skaldic diction, not a matching scene of singers dancing on a meadow; green adjectives are not cognate. Fragment/window boundaries further weaken the comparison.

Two genuine roots in a congruent narrative action, but the combination is unavoidable everyday description. Norse second partner places a log in a bed while the man sleeps elsewhere; no distinctive formula beyond ordinary lying and sleeping.
Russian носки in the second locus is adjacent to heels and can mean footwear tips; Latin is the wasting face of a sick person. No congruent formula established.

near_miss.lead: Lowering eyes to earth / striking earth with forehead
near_miss.why_not: Shared roots are distributed differently: sorrowful lowered gaze versus the physical fall of a dying man. The eye component in forehead does not preserve the same image or syntactic relations.

Russian locus is editorial prose citing a Christian cosmological poem; Latin is classical Oceanus. A common learned cosmography, including borrowed Ocean name, cannot establish independent inherited phrasing from these witnesses.
Only wind is a secure corresponding item; Russian rise has been mislemmatized as smoke, and Sanskrit become is not an epithet cognate in syntax with буйные. Shared storm subject is generic.

Three cognate word families but different attachment: Russian new sun versus Latin new lights of the sun. Modern celebratory imagery and physical renewal in Lucretius do not support inherited wording.

Russian Volga addresses a lake as sister, while RV 1.65.7a makes Agni a brother-like kinsman of rivers. RV 9.72.3d has two sets of sisters in a Soma context, not a demonstrably equivalent river/lake relation. Kin personification alone, with no cognate water term or predicate, remains insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Weapons shine like sun / shields gleam in sunlight
near_miss.why_not: Genuine shine and sun cognates, but Russian explicit simile is compared with Norse literal reflection of sunlight on shields. Natural optical description does not establish inherited phraseology.
Slab Sanskrit partner lists stages/material states with dry and cooking; it lacks grief. A closer external Ramayana witness is recorded as a search lead.
Slab Latin partner speaks of new temples of gods, not song. Wider Vedic search tests the closer formula separately.
The Atharvavedic slab partner invokes Indra without the eye/fire figure. Homer provides a closer external witness, recorded separately; no two-slab-anchor claim is made.

search_lead.cognate: Russian очи and Greek ὄσσε continue the eye word *h₃okʷ-. Fire nouns and burning predicates are renewed/noncognate here.
search_lead.argument: Russian очи огнемъ горятъ uses eyes as subject and fire in the instrumental; Homer has eyes blazing with fire, with πυρί dative. Both characterize an imposing figure, though the Russian snippet does not independently establish martial rage. A potentially traditional body/fire metaphor for review, not proof of inheritance.

search_lead.cognate: Russian Сушитъ and Sanskrit śuṣyati / śuṣyantīm continue the drying root *h₂sews-; the sorrow terminology is not asserted cognate.
search_lead.argument: The Russian line makes grief dry up the sufferer; the Ramayana describes grief-stricken wasting, including a lotus-withering comparison. This is a shared metaphor with causative/intransitive variation. Late Russian evidence and the natural metaphor require caution; the slab Sanskrit match itself is only literal dry material.

search_lead.cognate: Russian новую and Vedic návyam / návyebhiḥ belong to the inherited new-word family; song/praise nouns and production verbs are renewed.
search_lead.argument: The Russian exhortation to sing a new song and Vedic generation of new praise share the innovative-song motif. Only the adjective is cognate; Christian new-song diffusion and independent assertion of novelty remain alternatives for the late Russian witness. Recorded as a review lead, not a secure reconstruction.
